name: Jeffrey Epstein

summary.text: Jeffrey Epstein (1953-2019) was a U.S. financier who managed money and gave tax and estate advice to a few wealthy clients, chiefly Leslie Wexner and later Leon Black, largely through the Financial Trust Company he set up in the U.S. Virgin Islands. In 2008 he pleaded guilty to Florida state charges under a federal non-prosecution agreement that DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility later found reflected poor judgment but not misconduct. In July 2019 he was indicted in the Southern District of New York on sex-trafficking charges and died in federal custody on August 10, 2019; a 2023 DOJ Inspector General report found suicide enabled by jail staff failures. Afterwards New York's financial regulator fined Deutsche Bank $150 million over his accounts, JPMorgan Chase and Deutsche Bank paid $290 million and $75 million to settle victims' suits, and his estate paid the U.S. Virgin Islands more than $105 million.

Under it, he pleaded guilty on June 30, 2008 to Florida state charges; CNBC reported, citing his plea agreement, that the charges were procuring a person under 18 for prostitution and felony solicitation of prostitution.

facts.quote: While OPR did not find that Department attorneys engaged in professional misconduct, it concluded that the victims were not treated with the forthrightness and sensitivity expected by the Department.

facts.claim: Forbes reported, citing financial statements included in court records, that Epstein became a U.S. Virgin Islands resident in 1996, set up the Financial Trust Company there two years later, and that the firm generated $300 million in fee income from 2000 to 2006 while Wexner was a client, and less than $5 million over the following six years.

facts.claim: Documents reviewed by PBS NewsHour show Leslie Wexner gave Epstein his power of attorney in 1991, allowing Epstein to make investments, do business deals, buy property and help develop Wexner's New Albany, Ohio estate. Wexner revoked the power of attorney in 2007.
facts.quote: He gave his now-trusted associate his power of attorney in 1991, allowing Epstein to make investments and do business deals and to purchase property and help develop what would become the vast Wexner estate in then-rural New Albany, Ohio, documents show.

facts.claim: On July 7, 2020 the New York State Department of Financial Services announced a $150 million penalty on Deutsche Bank under a consent order covering its relationship with Epstein (August 2013 to December 2018) and its correspondent relationships with Danske Bank Estonia and FBME Bank. DFS called it the first enforcement action by a regulator against a financial institution for dealings with Epstein.
facts.quote: Deutsche Bank AG, its New York branch, and Deutsche Bank Trust Company America (collectively "Deutsche Bank" or the "Bank") have agreed to pay $150 million in penalties

facts.claim: The DFS consent order found that Deutsche Bank opened accounts on January 24, 2014 for an Epstein-related trust called The Butterfly Trust, that bank personnel knew at onboarding that a trust beneficiary was an alleged co-conspirator in Epstein's prior offenses, and that Epstein used the trust and other accounts to send over 120 wires totaling $2.65 million to trust beneficiaries. Conditions set by a reputational risk committee in January 2015 were not passed to most of the relationship team.
facts.quote: Conditions imposed by a Bank reputational risk committee were not transmitted to the majority of the account relationship team and were misinterpreted by a compliance officer.

CNN noted Epstein had been a Deutsche Bank client from 2013 to 2018 after 15 years as a JPMorgan Chase client.

facts.claim: In 2023 JPMorgan Chase agreed to pay $290 million to settle a class action by Epstein's victims and $75 million to settle the U.S. Virgin Islands' suit; the bank did not admit liability. In its summary-judgment motion the territory alleged that by Epstein's 2006 arrest the bank's compliance staff had noted he was 'known to pay cash for his massages' and that 'minors are the issue'; these were the territory's allegations, not findings.
facts.quote: By the time of Epstein's 2006 arrest for prostitution in Palm Beach, Florida, the company's compliance staff had been aware of alleged human trafficking and acknowledged Epstein was "known to pay cash for his massages" and "minors are the issue," the U.S. Virgin Islands alleges in its motion for summary judgment.

facts.claim: Steven Hoffenberg hired Epstein as a consultant to Towers Financial Corporation from about 1987 to 1993, paying him $25,000 a month and extending a $2 million loan in 1988 that Epstein did not have to repay, according to CBS News. Epstein left before the firm's collapse and was never charged in the Towers fraud.

facts.claim: Hoffenberg repeatedly asserted that Epstein was the 'architect' of the Towers Ponzi scheme, including in a 2016 suit seeking restitution for Towers victims and in 2019 interviews. The claim was never tested in court: his 2016 and 2018 suits were withdrawn, Epstein's lawyers called the claims untrue and time-barred, and no agency charged Epstein over Towers.

openQuestions: Hypothesis (a) 'where the money came from': sources support fees from Wexner (power of attorney 1991-2007; Financial Trust Company fee income of $300 million in 2000-2006 per court records cited by Forbes) and $158-170 million from Leon Black (Dechert review; Senate Finance Committee). The Towers Financial pay ($25,000/month plus a $2 million loan) is reported by CBS citing Hoffenberg-era accounts. No court or regulator has found that Towers money seeded Epstein's fortune.

Hypothesis (b) 'absorbed lost money from others' collapses': UNSUPPORTED by any court, regulator or official inquiry found. The only sources are Hoffenberg's own assertions and the withdrawn 2016/2018 suits (status: allegation). Wexner's 2019 'misappropriated' statement concerns Wexner's own money, not a collapse. No SEC action ever named Epstein over Towers.

Hypothesis (c) 'converted it to crypto': PARTLY supported only as ordinary venture investment: a ~$3 million 2014 Coinbase stake via IGO Company LLC (CoinDesk/Daily Herald, Feb 2026, citing unsealed DOJ files) and MIT Media Lab donations under Ito. No source shows Epstein moving client money, Towers money or Wexner money into cryptocurrency, holding significant Bitcoin, or that his estate inventory lists crypto. A crypto-news claim that he facilitated at least $750,000 to MIT's Digital Currency Initiative in 2017 was not verified against a primary document and is not recorded as a fact.

The OPR exhibit list and Cornell summary give the NPA date (Sept 24, 2007) and plea date (June 30, 2008); the exact Florida counts vary across secondary sources (one count of soliciting a minor vs. two counts) and the sentence (18 months imposed; about 13 served) should be checked against the plea agreement.
The date of Epstein's arrest: Berman's remarks say the previous Saturday (July 6, 2019); one later filing says July 8. The SDNY page and remarks are cited.

The $46 million Wexner figure comes from reporting (Forbes citing WSJ) on Wexner's letter, not from the letter text; Wexner has said it is only a portion. A later investigative memo reportedly says Epstein repaid $100 million; not verified here.

The DFS consent order PDF was not opened in full; the Butterfly Trust and wire figures come from the DFS press release and order excerpts returned by search. Whether the order uses the exact phrase 'known reputational risk' was not confirmed.
The $1 billion-plus JPMorgan processing figure originates in New York Times reporting on unsealed exhibits and in the Wyden staff memo; it is not a court finding.

Epstein's stake in Carbyne is indirect, through Barak's partnership; the size of the Epstein-linked contribution is not established by Haaretz ('a large part'). A Substack figure of $1 million is not used. No Bloomberg article on the Carbyne stake was returned.

The site's claims that Acosta said Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and that Epstein was 'intelligence-linked' were not found in any official record; the OPR report found no evidence the deal was based on Epstein's associations. Treat as unsupported.
Estate value (CBS: over $577 million; Forbes: nearly $600 million) is an estimate, not an audited figure; not recorded as a fact.
